top_choice_rationale: P001 recognises one identifiable invention, the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock (Katori) and its realisation at 10^-18 fractional uncertainty (Ye), with a short, undisputed two-name attribution, years of independent confirmation across laboratories and species, and demonstrated consequences for what can be measured (millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants, relativistic geodesy). It carries no maturity risk and the citation can be scoped to the lattice-clock architecture so ion-clock, comb and ultrastable-laser contributors are not demoted. P002 is scientifically spectacular and is my second choice, but its experimental credit is wider than the three names (Dean, the first author of the 2018 papers, Young, Yacoby, Efetov, Yazdani), the pairing mechanism is open after about eight years, and a prize must leave out people who did the measurements. Awarding a prize is still better than no award.
recusal_note: No specific conflict with Katori, Ye or the B022 laureates apparent from the profile. Kroll works in experimental atomic physics and quantum optics at Lund, the same broad field as the lattice clock, and has a documented research stay in John Hall's laboratory (Hall shared the 2005 prize for the frequency comb, which is outside the proposed citation); this is a field proximity, not a documented personal tie to the proposed laureates.
